name: Maya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Maya, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead carpenter for a small housing association builder, putting up timber-frame terraced houses on the edge of town, twelve at a time. The panels come in on a lorry and my crew stands them, sheathes them, fits the joists and the roof cassettes. Before I leave the house I've already had the AI on my phone check my cut list against the drawings, which saves me an hour of squinting most mornings. I love the speed of timber frame, a house standing in two days. What wears me out is the waiting, for the crane, the lorry, the inspector.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, and how does the money side look?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Hal hurt his back eleven years ago lifting a steel lintel, and now he works three days a week at the builders' merchant counter. Our daughter teaches in the city and our son does sound for a theatre. So it's mostly my wage, and the association pays less than the private builders. There's never more than a couple of weeks in the bank, honestly, and when the boiler went last winter it went on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say "well, that's a shame," which would get me some funny looks in the cabin. I'd probably post that it's still useful for the boring stuff, cut lists and orders, and leave it there. Most of the lads would be pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, and that's a mixed bag for me. My job's safe till I retire, but the pay stays low and so does the cushion. I was half hoping these tools would let a small crew like mine build cheaper homes faster, and that's what I'd miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same routine. I'd keep using the AI for drawings and quantities, keep running the crew, and keep paying the boiler card off at about eighty a month. I'd probably teach Junaid, my youngest carpenter, the tricks I use with it, because they'd still save him time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little flicker of disappointment, like a game called off for rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you be disappointed, when most of the crew would be pleased?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's a housing waiting list in this town as long as your arm, and I build the houses that would shorten it. If machines helped us put up forty a year instead of twenty-four, that's sixteen families. I'm not daft about who'd profit, but that's the part I care about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show Junaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to photograph the drawing and ask it for the stud spacing and the opening sizes, then check three of them by hand. Never trust it blind. Last month it told me a window opening was nine hundred when it was nine-sixty, and that would've been a fun morning.

S0.say: She'd say it's a shame, to some funny looks in the site cabin, and post that AI is still useful for boring tasks like cut lists and orders.
S0.think: Privately it's mixed: her job is safe till retirement, but pay and savings stay low. She'd miss the chance for small crews to build cheaper homes faster.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for drawings and quantities, keeps running the crew, and pays off the boiler card at about eighty a month. Teaches her youngest carpenter how she uses the tools, including checking a few figures by hand.
S0.feel: Calm, with a flicker of disappointment, like a game rained off.
S0.quote: If machines helped us put up forty a year instead of twenty-four, that's sixteen families.
S0.fieldNote: Unusually, she's disappointed by the plateau because she hoped AI would help build social housing faster. She uses the tools daily but checks them, and has a concrete story of an error she caught. Money is tight mainly because she's the main earner after her husband's injury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains go to the people doing the work. If robots stand panels, fine, but the crew should share the savings and the association should build more houses, not just cut wages. I'd say that at the union and to the association board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd do well out of it, as long as I'm early. I already use these tools every day. The risk is the firm uses it to make the crew smaller, and I end up the one person running machines while my mates are let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for any course on the new kit straight away, robotic nailing, the panel-standing rigs, whatever's coming, and I'd do it in my own time. I'd push the association to try it on one site with my crew, so we're the ones who learn it. And I'd keep paying down the card so I'm not in a hole if the hours wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, if I'm honest. A bit guilty about that excitement when I think of the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the course in your own time. Can you afford to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings, yes. A week off unpaid, no, not with Hal on three days. So it would have to be online or on Saturdays. I'd ask the union to push for paid release, but I wouldn't wait for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be guilty towards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, mostly. He's sixty-one and the best fixer I've ever worked with, and he won't touch a phone for anything but calls. I'd try to keep him on the bits he's brilliant at, the stairs and roof trims, but I know how firms think.

S1.say: She'd say the gains must go to workers: the crew should share the savings and the association should build more homes rather than cut wages. She'd tell both the union and the association board.
S1.think: Privately she expects to do well as an early adopter who already uses AI daily. Her fear is the firm shrinking the crew and leaving her running machines while mates are let go.
S1.do: Signs up for training on robotic nailing and panel rigs in her own evenings and Saturdays, and pushes the association to pilot the kit with her crew. Keeps paying down the card in case hours wobble.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with guilt when she thinks of older colleagues.
S1.quote: I'd ask the union to push for paid release, but I wouldn't wait for it.
S1.fieldNote: She combines union politics with a strong personal drive to adopt early. Thin savings shape how she can learn, evenings rather than unpaid weeks. Her guilt about Pete, a 61-year-old colleague, is real and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public ownership of this, now. If machines can build houses, then the council should own the machines and build homes for everyone, not hand it all to three companies. I'd be at the protests and on every forum I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, being early doesn't save me much here. Full AGI with robots means the clever bits I do with the tools get done without me too. Maybe I'm the last person kept on to watch the machines for a year, and then what, at sixty, with nothing saved?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the association in the first month and offer to run the pilot, because the person who runs it stays longest. I'd talk to Pete and two others about forming a co-op, a small firm that owns a robot rig and builds for the council, if there's any public money for that. And I'd stop the card spending and get Hal to ask for more days at the merchant's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, which helps, but there's a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' warning, what would you do in those two years before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn everything I can and get my name known as the one who knows the machines. Save every penny I can, which might be two thousand if we're lucky. Two years is long enough to get in position, not long enough to build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A co-op owning a robot rig. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't, not without help. That's the honest answer. It would need a public grant or a council contract up front, and I'd lobby for exactly that.

S2.say: She'd demand public ownership: if machines can build houses, councils should own them and build homes for everyone. She'd join protests and argue online.
S2.think: Privately she sees that being early buys little against full AGI; maybe a year as the last person minding the machines, then out at 60 with no savings.
S2.do: Offers to run the association's robot pilot in the first month and talks to colleagues about a worker co-op that owns a robot rig, lobbying for public money to fund it. Stops card spending and asks her husband to seek more days.
S2.feel: Anxious, with busyness keeping a knot in her stomach at bay.
S2.quote: Two years is long enough to get in position, not long enough to build a cushion.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability gives her a plan, but she's honest that early adoption only delays the outcome under full AGI. The co-op idea depends entirely on public money, which she admits. Her politics move to public ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set things up properly, and I'd say it hard: housing co-ops, public robot fleets, retraining that's paid. We've had warning, so let's not waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a better shape for me. Sixty-three when it lands, and I might get three or four years as the person who runs the machines on site. It's still close to the pension and still thin on savings, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get trained on everything and run the first pilot. Years two and three, I'd try to start the co-op properly, with a council contract, Pete and Junaid in it. And I'd pay off the card and start a small savings pot, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of energy. It feels like something I could have a hand in shaping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the co-op, really. Two years, it's a dream. Five, I could actually get a contract and a few jobs under our belt before the big firms swamp everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Junaid is young. What would you tell him to do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the machines and the software, yes, but also learn to talk to clients and councils. When the hands-on bit goes, the person who knows how a house should go together and can explain it will still be useful a while longer.

S3.say: She'd push hard for housing co-ops, public robot fleets and paid retraining, saying five years of warning must not be wasted.
S3.think: Privately it's a better shape: 63 when it arrives and maybe three or four years running machines on site, though savings stay thin.
S3.do: Trains on the new kit and runs the first pilot in year one, then sets up a co-op with two colleagues around a council contract in years two and three. Pays off the card and starts saving fifty a month.
S3.feel: Uneasy but full of energy, feeling she could help shape it.
S3.quote: Two years, it's a dream. Five, I could actually get a contract and a few jobs under our belt before the big firms swamp everything.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn her co-op idea from a wish into a plan. Her advice to a young colleague focuses on understanding and explaining how a house goes together. She is calmer here than with two years, largely because she has room to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. We could plan the whole thing: build the homes we need, train people, share what the machines make. I'd be arguing for that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly about finishing well. I'd be sixty-eight, so I'd probably want to wind down by then anyway. The worry is Hal and me living on a small pension with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the crew and learning the new kit as it comes. Somewhere in the middle, I'd help train the next lot on the machines, maybe teach at the college two evenings a week for the extra money. And I'd save what I could, which still isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, hopeful about everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching at the college. Have you thought about that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college asked me two years ago and I said no, because of the hours. In this picture it makes sense, it's extra money and it gets me ahead of it. And I'd enjoy it, telling teenagers how a house really stands up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the robots mean for your kids, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter teaches, and I think people will still want a human with their kids, but I don't know. My son does theatre sound, and that might be gone sooner than my job. I'd tell them both to watch it closely and not wait.

S4.say: She'd call ten years a gift and argue everywhere for planning: building needed homes, training people and sharing what machines produce.
S4.think: Privately it's about finishing well; at 68 she'd be winding down, but she worries about living with her husband on a small pension and no savings.
S4.do: Keeps running the crew and learning new kit, then takes evening teaching at the local college for extra money and to train others on the machines. Saves what little she can.
S4.feel: Uneasy about money, hopeful about everything else.
S4.quote: And I'd enjoy it, telling teenagers how a house really stands up.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her focus moves from survival to finishing well and teaching. Money worries persist in every scenario because of her single main income. She thinks her son's job may go before hers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I can't learn, but because nobody else would have time to set up the public side, the co-ops and the council fleets, and it all goes to whoever owns the machines already. What would help is public money to let workers own the robots, and a bridge to the pension for people my age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd build if the machines were ours. Houses, hundreds of them, for the people on the waiting list. That's what I'd want this whole thing to be for.

headlineQuote: Maybe I'm the last person kept on to watch the machines for a year, and then what, at sixty, with nothing saved?
portrait: Maya Rahman is a 58-year-old lead carpenter on timber-frame social housing who checks her cut lists with AI every morning and is the main earner since her husband's back injury. She hoped AI would help build homes faster and is almost disappointed by a plateau. She would jump on new kit early in steady change, but under AGI in two years she knows being early only buys a little time, and her co-op idea needs public money she doesn't have. With five or ten years she has room to start a co-op, teach at the college and finish her working life well, though thin savings worry her throughout.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to set up public ownership or co-ops and everything would go to whoever already owns the machines.
whatWouldHelp: Public money so workers can own the robots, and a bridge to the pension for people her age.
